reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma
clinicalPearls: Caused by a developmental abnormality of the trabecular meshwork and angle (trabeculodysgenesis) that obstructs aqueous outflow, often with autosomal recessive inheritance linked to the CYP1B1 gene
The classic triad of presentation is epiphora (watering), photophobia, and blepharospasm in an infant
Because the immature sclera and cornea are distensible, raised pressure enlarges the globe, producing an abnormally large cornea and eye (buphthalmos)
Stretching of the cornea splits Descemet membrane, creating curvilinear Haab striae, and causes corneal oedema and clouding
Examination often requires assessment under anaesthesia to measure pressure, corneal diameter, and axial length and to perform gonioscopy and disc evaluation
Optic-disc cupping can enlarge rapidly in infants and may partially reverse once pressure is controlled
Treatment is primarily surgical, with angle procedures such as goniotomy or trabeculotomy to open the obstructed drainage pathway, and medical therapy used as a temporising adjunct
It must be distinguished from other causes of a large or cloudy infant cornea and from secondary and syndromic developmental glaucomas
reference.pathophysiology: Primary congenital glaucoma arises from maldevelopment of the anterior chamber angle, in which abnormal differentiation of the trabecular meshwork and related tissues impairs aqueous outflow and raises intraocular pressure. Many cases are autosomal recessive and associated with mutations in the CYP1B1 gene. Because the collagen of an infant's cornea and sclera is still elastic, sustained pressure elevation stretches the whole globe, enlarging the corneal diameter and axial length to produce buphthalmos. Rapid corneal stretching ruptures Descemet membrane, giving the horizontal or curvilinear breaks known as Haab striae, and causes corneal oedema. The developing optic nerve is vulnerable, and cupping can progress quickly but may partly reverse after successful pressure control.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital corneal opacities such as sclerocornea or birth-related Descemet tears
Developmental glaucomas with anterior segment dysgenesis (Axenfeld-Rieger, Peters anomaly, aniridia)
Secondary infantile glaucoma from intrauterine inflammation or trauma
additionalInvestigations: Examination under anaesthesia with intraocular pressure measurement
Corneal diameter and axial length measurement to document enlargement
Optic disc assessment for cup-to-disc ratio, with photography or imaging where possible
Refraction and assessment for amblyopia and anisometropia
Genetic evaluation, including CYP1B1 testing and assessment for syndromic associations when indicated
redFlags: Progressive corneal enlargement or clouding indicating uncontrolled pressure needing urgent surgery
Rapidly increasing optic-disc cupping in an infant
The triad of watering, photophobia, and blepharospasm prompting immediate specialist referral
Asymmetric or unilateral globe enlargement risking severe amblyopia
reference.prognosis: With early angle surgery many eyes achieve good long-term pressure control and useful vision, but outcomes worsen with late presentation, marked corneal clouding, and high pressures; amblyopia, refractive error, and corneal scarring commonly limit final vision even after successful pressure control.
pitfalls: Attributing infant watering solely to nasolacrimal duct obstruction and missing glaucoma
Overlooking early buphthalmos because both eyes are symmetrically enlarged
Relying on medical therapy alone when the definitive treatment is surgical
Failing to manage amblyopia and refractive error alongside pressure control
Mistaking Haab striae or corneal oedema for a primary corneal disorder
management: Definitive treatment is angle surgery, goniotomy or trabeculotomy, to relieve the trabeculodysgenesis and lower intraocular pressure; this is the primary intervention
Use topical and systemic pressure-lowering agents such as carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, beta-blockers and prostaglandin analogues as a temporising bridge to surgery or as adjuncts
Proceed to further glaucoma surgery, such as trabeculectomy, a drainage implant or cyclodestruction, for eyes not controlled by initial angle surgery
Perform examination under anaesthesia to serially monitor intraocular pressure, corneal diameter, axial length and optic disc cupping
Treat amblyopia and correct refractive error, which commonly limit vision even after successful pressure control
Offer genetic counselling including CYP1B1 testing and assess for syndromic associations
Refer to a paediatric glaucoma specialist for lifelong surveillance, as pressure control can fail over time
